meta.title: OpenMCPGateway — auth, limits and logs in front of any MCP server
meta.description: OpenMCPGateway puts auth, authorisation, rate limiting and a full request log in front of any MCP server. One endpoint per server, an identity provider you already run, and a call log that answers who used this and what broke.
hero.title: Auth, limits and logs in front of any MCP server.
hero.lead: An MCP server ships with one static token pasted into every client, or with no auth at all because it sits on a private network. Both fail the moment the server is worth using: the token cannot be revoked per person, and “on the private network” is one misrouted Service away from the internet.
hero.lead2: Point the client at the gateway instead. It terminates the login or verifies a bearer key, checks that the caller belongs to the gateway's tenant, enforces a per-caller budget, and records every call with its payload.
hero.note: Live deployment: mcp-gateway.giomartins.dev. The manual is on this site and needs no account.
hero.shotAlt: The traffic page: a flow chart of gateways and outcomes, outcome totals, and a table of individual calls.
hero.shotCap: Traffic — every call is a row: gateway, subject, outcome, status, tool, latency and IP. The flow chart says where the traffic went; the table says which call it was.
how.title: Three decisions, in this order
how.lead: The gateway does not care what your MCP server does. It decides who reaches it, how often, and leaves a record of what happened.
how.s1.title: Point it at your server
how.s1.body: Give the gateway a slug and the upstream MCP URL. The upstream stays unreachable from outside; the gateway is the only door.
how.s2.title: Choose who gets in
how.s2.body: No auth for a private network, a bearer key for machines, or SSO for people — GitHub, Google, Microsoft, Discord, any OIDC provider, or the gateway's own identity provider when you have none. Each gateway decides for itself, and one gateway can accept keys and logins at once.
how.s3.title: Paste the endpoint
how.s3.body: You paste /g/<slug>/mcp into the client. For OAuth, the client discovers the rest from the 401 challenge on its own. Every tenant starts with one gateway already there: the deployment's own read-only console.

feat.title: What it does, and what it refuses
feat.lead: Fail closed is the default: an OAuth gateway with no credentials answers 503, never as an open proxy. Everything below is visible in the panel, because a control you cannot audit is a control you cannot defend.
feat.f1.title: Identity you already have
feat.f1.body: GitHub, Google, Microsoft, Discord or any OIDC provider — or the gateway's own provider, so a self-hosted install with no IdP still gets SSO. Who may call is decided by the tenant that owns the gateway, read fresh on every request.
feat.f2.title: One endpoint per MCP server
feat.f2.body: Clients point at /g/<slug>/mcp. The gateway terminates OAuth or verifies a bearer key, then calls the real server over the private network with an upstream credential the caller never holds.
feat.f3.title: Per-caller budgets
feat.f3.body: Requests per minute per subject, counting JSON-RPC calls only — handshakes and notifications are free — plus an optional monthly quota. Redis-backed when you run more than one replica.
feat.f4.title: Every call is a row
feat.f4.body: Subject, outcome, status, latency, IP, tool name and a capped payload trace with the request and the response, appended to an event log that backs both the traffic table and the audit trail.
feat.f5.title: Panel and file are the same
feat.f5.body: Export the tenant to YAML, edit it, apply it back. Both paths reach one command handler, so they cannot disagree — and the panel shows the diff before an apply.
feat.f6.title: A console you can ask
feat.f6.body: Every tenant ships with a gateway to this deployment's own read-only MCP. Point an agent at /g/console/mcp and ask what broke, or what the audit log says.
screens.title: The panel, screen by screen
screens.lead: One control surface for gateways, keys, members and traffic. Light is the default and dark is one click away, built from the same tokens — no screen is styled twice.
screens.s1.title: Every gateway on one line
screens.s1.body: Slug, auth mode, upstream state and the traffic it is taking. The list filters and sorts under each column header, and a cursor keeps the page honest no matter how many rows the tenant has.
screens.s2.title: One gateway, in full
screens.s2.body: The endpoint to paste, the auth mode, each upstream tool with how often it was called, the allowlist, and a connect guide generated from the live proxy configuration.
screens.s3.title: The call behind the row
screens.s3.body: Outcome, subject, latency, and the request and response bodies shaped as JSON — one click from the raw bytes. This is where “403” turns into a sentence.
screens.s4.title: Light and dark, one palette
screens.s4.body: The same traffic page with the dark tokens. Neither theme is an afterthought, because neither is a filter painted over the other.
run.title: Run it yourself
run.lead: One compose file, Postgres included. The first account to register becomes the deployment's admin, and every tenant starts with a working read-only console gateway, so there is something to call before you wire anything up.
